name: Spotlight effect
statement: People think others notice them far more than others do, so an embarrassing shirt or a stumbled sentence feels public when it was barely registered.
meaning: The claim is about a gap between two quantities that can both be measured: how much attention you believe you are getting and how much you are actually getting. Because your own appearance and behaviour are the most available thing in your own head, you start from that vivid impression and adjust downward for the fact that others have their own concerns. The adjustment is too small, which is anchoring applied to yourself. The design that makes this testable is the one that measures both sides in the same room at the same time.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is "The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance", and it gave the phenomenon its name.

evidence: A participant was asked to put on a T-shirt with a large picture of Barry Manilow, chosen because Cornell undergraduates found it embarrassing, and was then sent into a room of other participants. Afterwards they estimated what fraction of the room could say who was on the shirt. They said 46%. The observers were asked separately, and 23% could. The targets' estimates were also higher than those of control participants who were simply told what was on the shirt, F(2, 42) = 5.76. Two further details make the mechanism visible: in a later study the estimate was 48% against an actual 8%, and participants given a delay to get used to wearing the shirt estimated 37% where those sent straight in estimated 51%.

replication.headline: No replication attempt was found, which for a paradigm this widely taught is worth stating plainly.

limits: The search that produced this verdict covered the Wikipedia article's reference list, Crossref, and web searches for preregistered or multi-laboratory replications of Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky. It came up empty. That is a statement about what was found rather than proof that nothing exists: this literature has no equivalent of the Many Labs projects to check against, and a targeted database search through PsycINFO or the Open Science Framework could turn something up that these searches missed. The original studies also used small samples in one university, and the effect sizes are reported as percentages and F values rather than in a standardised form, so there is no figure here to compare a future replication against.
misreadings: The effect is usually passed on as reassurance, that nobody is looking at you, which is stronger than the finding. Almost a quarter of the room did identify the shirt. What was measured is a gap between 46% and 23%, so the accurate summary is that people notice you about half as much as you think, not that they do not notice you. The effect is also routinely merged with the illusion of transparency, the belief that your inner states are visible, which is a related claim from the same authors and a separate body of evidence.

sources.text: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., & Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.
